name.text: Angle between two lines in a cuboid

questiontext.text:
In the cuboid ABCDEFGH, AB = {@ll@} cm, BC = {@ww@} cm and AE = {@hh@} cm.

(a) Which triangle contains both {@L1@} and {@L2@}? Triangle

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Find angle {@nm@}.

[[input:ans2]] \(^\circ\) [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

Give lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer.

generalfeedback.text:
(a) {@L1@} and {@L2@} both start at {@PV@}; the third side joins their other ends, {@XY@}. So the triangle is {@tri@}.

[[if test="rt"]]

(b) Triangle {@tri@} has a right angle at {@RR@}: an edge of the triangle is at right angles to a face that contains another side. \({@PR@}^2 = {@qR@}\) and \({@HY@}^2 = {@qH@}\), so \(\cos {@nm@} = \frac{{@PR@}}{{@HY@}} = \frac{\sqrt{{@qR@}}}{\sqrt{{@qH@}}}\), and angle {@nm@} = \({@d1(th)@}^\circ\).

[[else]]

(b) Triangle {@tri@} has no right angle. By Pythagoras, \({@PX@}^2 = {@qX@}\), \({@PY@}^2 = {@qY@}\) and \({@XY@}^2 = {@qXY@}\). The cosine rule gives \(\cos {@nm@} = \frac{{@qX@} + {@qY@} - {@qXY@}}{2 \times \sqrt{{@qX@}} \times \sqrt{{@qY@}}}\), so angle {@nm@} = \({@d1(th)@}^\circ\).

[[/if]]

questiondescription.text:
Three-Dimensional Geometry: angle between two lines in a cuboid

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.4: Name the triangle that contains two lines meeting at a vertex of a cuboid, then find the angle between them, with or without a right angle.

Core

This question is adapted from Chapter 34, Section A, questions A6 and A10 of Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP GCSE Mathematics: Higher 2 for AQA, Edexcel and OCR two-tier GCSE mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 2007: new lines, cuboids and wording, a naming step, right-angled and cosine-rule cases, randomised, with named feedback.

truefeedback.text: That is angle {@oA@}, the angle at {@charat(oA,2)@}. The angle you want is at {@PV@}, opposite the side {@XY@}.
That is angle {@oB@}, the angle at {@YY@}. The angle you want is at {@PV@}, opposite the side {@XY@}.
This triangle has no right angle, so the angles do not add to \(90^\circ\) in pairs: use the cosine rule with {@XY@} opposite angle {@nm@}.
